title: List of football stadiums in Germany — Grokipedia
content: The list of football stadiums in Germany encompasses a comprehensive catalog of venues primarily used for association football, ordered by capacity and including grounds from professional leagues like the Bundesliga down to notable regional facilities, with over 60 stadiums exceeding 10,000 spectators.](#ref-1) These stadiums reflect Germany's status as a global football powerhouse, hosting major competitions such as the FIFA World Cup 2006 and UEFA EURO 2024 across ten world-class venues, including the Olympiastadion in Berlin and the Volksparkstadion in Hamburg.](#ref-2) Among the most prominent are modern arenas built or extensively renovated in the early 2000s to meet international standards, particularly in preparation for the 2006 FIFA World Cup, which spurred infrastructure upgrades across the country.](#ref-3) The largest, **Signal Iduna Park** in Dortmund, boasts a capacity of 81,365 and is renowned for its iconic standing terrace, the Yellow Wall, drawing massive crowds for Borussia Dortmund matches.](#ref-4) Following closely is the **Allianz Arena** in Munich with 75,024 seats, a technologically advanced venue home to FC Bayern Munich and celebrated for its illuminated exterior.](#ref-5) Other key stadiums include the Olympiastadion Berlin (74,475 capacity), a historic site from the 1936 Olympics that hosted EURO 2024's final, and the Veltins-Arena in Gelsenkirchen (62,271), featuring a retractable roof and pitch.](#ref-1) This diverse array of stadiums, many of which are "pure football" designs without athletics tracks, underscores the sport's deep cultural integration in Germany, supporting over 24,000 clubs and 7.7 million members nationwide.](#ref-6) The list highlights not only capacity and location but also architectural innovations and historical significance, from post-war reconstructions to contemporary sustainability features seen in venues like the MHPArena in Stuttgart.](#ref-7).

content: # Bundesliga Stadiums. The popularity of soccer in Germany and around the world means that stadiums need to hold huge crowds. Temple, church, arena – soccer stadiums can sometimes feel like a second home to many fans. Every weekend, hundreds or even thousands of fans flock to their closest soccer stadium to cheer on their favorite team – or indeed, travel hundreds of miles to do just that at away games. In Germany, you can visit many amazing soccer stadiums where Bundesliga matches are held, including the historic Olympic Stadium in Berlin, Bremen’s Weser Stadium, the ultra-modern Allianz Arena in Munich or the Westfalen Stadium (also known as the Signal Iduna Park) in Dortmund, which is the biggest stadium in Germany. *There is a phenomenon called “groundhopping” in which participating fans will try to visit as many stadiums as possible.
